screens.title: Legacy Input Manager — What it is and when to use it
screens.narratorSegment: The legacy Input Manager is Unity's built-in, polling-based input system. Polling means you ask the A P I each frame whether a key or button is down or whether an axis has a value. Common calls include GetKey, GetKeyDown, GetKeyUp, GetMouseButton variants, and GetAxis for named axes like Horizontal and Vertical. This system is fast to start with and good for small projects or prototypes where remapping and multi-device routing are not critical. A concrete example: you can poll Input. GetKeyDown for the space key to detect a jump press in the same frame it occurred. One important detail is that GetKeyDown and GetButtonDown are frame-based and should be read in Update so you don't miss presses. Areas where the legacy manager can cause friction include remapping, supporting many controllers, or splitting controls across many players; these require custom glue and can become error-prone. A common misconception is that GetAxis always returns immediate raw input; by default it smooths values, so GetAxisRaw exists when you need unsmoothed results. Key takeaway: use the legacy A P I for fast prototypes and simple single-player controls, but plan to move to the Input System if you need device-agnostic maps, remapping, or robust multi-player support.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Legacy Input Manager
Definition
Polling API for keys, buttons, and axes
You query the API each frame for input state using Input class methods. It's straightforward but less flexible for remapping and multi-device setups.
• Use GetKeyDown and GetButtonDown to detect presses that occur in a single frame.
• Use GetAxis for named axes such as Horizontal and Vertical; smoothing is applied unless you use GetAxisRaw.
• Read frame-based calls inside Update to avoid missed input events.
Concrete example
Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") triggers a jump the frame the player presses space when Jump is configured in Project Settings.
Common misconception
GetAxis is not always raw input; it can be smoothed. Use GetAxisRaw for immediate values.
Key Takeaway

Legacy input is simple and reliable for small projects, but plan for migration if you need remapping or robust multi-device support.

Quick reference
// Polling example
if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump")){
  // trigger jump
}
float h = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
float v = Input.GetAxisRaw("Vertical");
Why this matters
Understanding the legacy API helps you read older projects and prototype quickly. It also establishes the timing rules you'll need when migrating to event-driven callbacks.
Try this
Create a cube, add a Rigidbody, and use Input.GetAxis to move it. Then compare smoothed and raw axis values while holding and releasing keys.

screens.title: Reading input correctly: Update, FixedUpdate, and polling timing
screens.narratorSegment: A common source of bugs is mixing input polling timing with physics updates. Unity provides Update for per-frame logic and FixedUpdate for physics steps. For the legacy Input Manager, methods like GetKeyDown and GetButtonDown should be read in Update because they are frame-accurate. If you read them in FixedUpdate you risk missing presses because FixedUpdate may run fewer times per frame or at different intervals. For movement, a typical pattern is to read axis values in Update and store them, then apply movement in FixedUpdate where physics calculations happen. In the new Input System, event-driven callbacks deliver input events reliably and decouple when you read them from when you apply them. Still, apply physics changes like adding force or MovePosition in FixedUpdate, using the last known input state captured in a callback or stored in a field. A concrete pattern: capture the Vector2 movement from the Move action into a field, then in FixedUpdate construct a world movement and call rb. MovePosition with Time. fixedDeltaTime. A misconception to avoid is assuming callbacks automatically occur on the physics thread; they are still delivered on the main thread, so you must control where you apply forces. Key takeaway: read input at the right time, store intent, and apply physics in FixedUpdate to ensure deterministic simulation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Input Timing & Physics
Rule
Read input timing, apply physics later
Read button presses and axes in Update or capture them via Input System callbacks. Apply movement forces and position changes in FixedUpdate to keep physics deterministic.
1. Read frame inputs with GetKeyDown or Input System callbacks.
2. Store the intent (vector or button press) in a field.
3. In FixedUpdate, use stored values to call rb.MovePosition or AddForce.
Example pattern
// capture in Update or callback
currentMovement = ReadMovement();

// apply in FixedUpdate
rb.MovePosition(rb.position + move * Time.fixedDeltaTime);
Pitfall
Reading GetKeyDown in FixedUpdate can miss single-frame presses because FixedUpdate may not execute every frame. Store intent in Update instead.
Pro tip
For the new Input System, set callbacks to update fields and use those fields during physics updates. This keeps event handling and physics consistent.
Check your understanding
If a jump press sometimes fails to register when using FixedUpdate, what likely caused it? Reflect on timing rules.

screens.title: Axes, GetAxis, and GetAxisRaw
screens.narratorSegment: Axes are logical, named controls you configure in Project Settings under the Input Manager. A common axis is Horizontal which can aggregate multiple physical inputs: arrow keys, A/D, or a joystick X-axis. When you use Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") Unity returns a float between minus one and one. By default Unity applies smoothing to axis values, which helps make character movement feel less abrupt. If you need immediate, unsmoothed input for twitchy or pixel-precise controls, use Input. GetAxisRaw("Horizontal") which returns the raw device value. Another useful legacy pattern is to map a button to an axis name and use Input. GetButton or GetButtonDown with that name for actions. An important practical example: combining a keyboard composite and joystick axis under the same axis name lets you write movement code that is device-agnostic at runtime. The key misconception is assuming axis values are identical across devices; sensitivity and dead zone settings differ and must be tuned in the Input Manager. Key takeaway: axes simplify access to multiple bindings under a single name, but be deliberate about smoothing and tuning for responsiveness. Axes, GetAxis, and GetAxisRaw means use named axes to unify device inputs; choose getaxisraw when you need unsmoothed, immediate values for tight control.. In practical terms, how named axes work and when to use raw values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Axes & GetAxis
Concept
Named axes unify multiple bindings
An axis like Horizontal can map to keys and to a gamepad stick. GetAxis returns a smoothed float; GetAxisRaw returns the unsmoothed value.
• Use GetAxis when you want smoothing for natural movement.
• Use GetAxisRaw for responsive, immediate control.
• Tune sensitivity and dead zones in Project Settings to match expected device behavior.
Quick example
float h = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
float v = Input.GetAxisRaw("Vertical");
Vector3 move = new Vector3(h, 0, v);
transform.Translate(move * speed * Time.deltaTime);
Why this matters
Choosing the right axis method affects feel. For platformers or tight movement, prefer raw values; for smooth camera or character acceleration, prefer smoothed axis values.
Try it
Switch between GetAxis and GetAxisRaw and observe how acceleration and instant stops differ while walking and stopping with keyboard keys.

screens.title: LegacyPlayerInput example explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided LegacyPlayerInput example and highlight the teaching points. The script acquires a Rigidbody in Start and disables itself if absent — a defensive pattern to avoid null references at runtime. Input polling happens in Update because GetButtonDown and GetMouseButtonDown are frame-based queries. The code reads horizontal and vertical axes using Input. GetAxis and composes a move vector before applying Translate. For jump, the script checks Input. GetButtonDown("Jump") which maps to the spacebar by default in the Input Manager; the example then applies an impulse using AddForce on the Rigidbody. Mouse left-button polling uses Input. GetMouseButtonDown(0) to trigger a fire action. Notice that using transform. Translate for desktop-style movement is quick for simple prototypes but bypasses physics-driven movement; mixing Translate with physics bodies can produce non-physical results. If you want to apply forces or move a Rigidbody, do so in FixedUpdate using rb. MovePosition or AddForce. A common misconception is to treat Update and FixedUpdate interchangeably; they are not. The concrete takeaway: use Update to poll input, prefer physics APIs in FixedUpdate, and use the Rigidbody safely to manage colliders and forces. Try modifying the demo to use rb. MovePosition in FixedUpdate and observe collision behavior changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Legacy Code Walkthrough
Example script
using UnityEngine;

public class LegacyPlayerInput : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5f;
    public float jumpForce = 10f;

    private Rigidbody rb;

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent();
        if (rb == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("Rigidbody missing!");
            enabled = false;
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        float horizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        float vertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector3 moveDirection = new Vector3(horizontal, 0, vertical);
        transform.Translate(moveDirection * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);

        if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump"))
        {
            rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
        }

        if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0))
        {
            Debug.Log("Fire!");
        }
    }
}
Annotations
  • Start(): defensive null check for Rigidbody to avoid runtime errors.
  • Update(): polls GetAxis and GetButtonDown; suitable for frame-accurate input.
  • Movement: uses transform.Translate — easy but not always physics-friendly.
  • Jump: AddForce on Rigidbody — physics-based action applied immediately when detected.
Practice change
Replace transform.Translate with stored input applied in FixedUpdate via rb.MovePosition to observe consistent physics behavior.

screens.narratorSegment: Transitioning to the new Input System begins with the Package Manager. Next, create an Input Actions asset in the Project window. The asset is where Action Maps, Actions, and Bindings live. Create an action map named Gameplay or Player for in-game controls, and add Actions like Move, Jump, and Fire. For Move, choose Action Type Value and Control Type Vector2; add a WASD composite and a gamepad left stick binding. For Jump and Fire choose Button type and add keyboard and gamepad bindings. Save the asset. A common misconception is that installing the package is enough; you must also enable the new backend when prompted or project input may still run through the legacy pipeline. Key takeaway: the new Input System is data-driven — the asset drives the runtime behavior, so organizing your Actions and Action Maps clearly up front simplifies wiring controls later with PlayerInput or code. Installing and setting up the New Input System means install package, accept backend switch, create input actions asset, define action maps, actions and bindings.. In practical terms, package install, enable backend, and create an input actions asset. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › New Input System Setup
Steps
  1. Open Window → Package Manager and install Input System from the Unity Registry.
  2. Accept Unity's prompt to enable the new input backend and restart the editor if required.
  3. Right-click in Project window → Create → Input Actions to make an Input Action asset.
  4. Open the asset and add an Action Map named Gameplay or Player.
  5. Add Actions: Move (Value, Vector2), Jump (Button), Fire (Button). Add WASD composite and gamepad bindings for Move.
Key Takeaway
The asset is the canonical definition of your controls; treat it like configuration rather than code.
Bindings example
Move action: add a 2D Vector composite with Up=W, Down=S, Left=A, Right=D. Then add a binding for Gamepad Left Stick. Jump action: add Space and Gamepad A. Fire: Left Mouse Button and Gamepad Right Trigger.
Misconception
Installing the package without enabling the backend leaves the project on the legacy pipeline. Always accept the switch when prompted for new projects.

screens.title: Input Action Asset, Action Maps, Actions, and Bindings
screens.narratorSegment: The Input System uses a small set of concepts to represent controls: an Input Action Asset is a scriptable object that contains Action Maps. Each Action Map groups actions relevant to a context — for example, Player gameplay actions versus UI navigation. An Action represents a discrete game behavior like Move, Jump, or Fire. Actions have types; common choices are Button, Value, and Pass-Through. Bindings connect an action to physical controls such as keys, mouse buttons, or joystick axes. A Move action of type Value with control type Vector2 typically has a WASD composite binding and a separate binding for the gamepad left stick. This design separates control configuration from code: scripts respond to Action events or read Action values, and the same action can be re-bound without changing code. A useful analogy is thinking of Actions as public methods and bindings as the remappable keys that call them. A common misuse is scattering bindings across multiple assets or failing to group related actions into coherent maps, which hampers enabling or disabling sets of controls by context. Key takeaway: design clear action maps aligned with game states and keep action names meaningful so designers and programmers can collaborate without editing code.

narration.text: The Input System uses a small set of concepts to represent controls: an Input Action Asset is a scriptable object that contains Action Maps. Each Action Map groups actions relevant to a context — for example, Player gameplay actions versus UI navigation. An Action represents a discrete game behavior like Move, Jump, or Fire. Actions have types; common choices are Button, Value, and Pass-Through. Bindings connect an action to physical controls such as keys, mouse buttons, or joystick axes. A Move action of type Value with control type Vector2 typically has a WASD composite binding and a separate binding for the gamepad left stick. This design separates control configuration from code: scripts respond to Action events or read Action values, and the same action can be re-bound without changing code. A useful analogy is thinking of Actions as public methods and bindings as the remappable keys that call them. A common misuse is scattering bindings across multiple assets or failing to group related actions into coherent maps, which hampers enabling or disabling sets of controls by context. Key takeaway: design clear action maps aligned with game states and keep action names meaningful so designers and programmers can collaborate without editing code.

keyIdea.title: Asset anatomy
keyIdea.text: Input Action Asset → Action Maps → Actions → Bindings. Keep maps contextual and actions descriptive to simplify runtime switching and remapping.

Hierarchy
Asset → Action Maps → Actions → Bindings
This layered structure lets you encapsulate controls and switch contexts at runtime without changing code. Keep maps aligned with states like Gameplay, UI, or Driving.

Scriptable object holding all maps and bindings.

Contextual collection like Gameplay or UI.
Binding

Design example
Create a Player map; add Move (Vector2) with WASD and left stick, Jump (Button) with Space and gamepad A, Fire (Button) with left mouse and right trigger. This keeps gameplay bindings grouped and easy to enable or disable.

screens.title: Using the PlayerInput component
screens.narratorSegment: The PlayerInput component simplifies using the new Input System. Attach it to your player GameObject, drag the Input Actions asset into the Actions field, and choose a Behavior. Behavior options include Invoke Unity Events, Invoke C# Events, and Send Messages. For beginners, Invoke Unity Events is easiest because you can link actions to public methods in the Inspector without writing event subscription code. After selecting Invoke Unity Events, expand the action map and add listeners for Move, Jump, and Fire, mapping them to methods like OnMove, OnJump, and OnFire on your player script. The PlayerInput component also automatically enables and disables the action map as the component toggles, helping with context switching. If you have multiple players, PlayerInput can be configured to pair with a specific device, which helps route each controller to the correct player. A misconception is thinking PlayerInput writes your callback wiring for you; it merely provides convenient event dispatch — you still implement the methods that react to those events. Key takeaway: PlayerInput makes wiring actions quick and supports different invocation patterns; use it to reduce boilerplate while you prototype action handling.

screens.title: NewPlayerInput and callbacks: OnMove, OnJump, OnFire
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough explains how a player script handles Input System callbacks. The example script stores the last Vector2 movement received in OnMove by calling context. ReadValue (). That value represents the player's intended horizontal and vertical motion. In FixedUpdate the script converts this Vector2 into a world-space vector and calls rb. MovePosition or uses AddForce for physics-based movement. For button-style actions like Jump and Fire, use context. performed to ensure you react only when the action is fully invoked, avoiding responded-to started or canceled phases. For Jump, check if the player is grounded before applying an impulse to prevent mid-air multi-jumps. Use OnCollisionEnter and OnCollisionExit to maintain a simple grounded flag. A common contrast with polling is that callbacks provide the exact moment of input and reduce the need to query every frame, but you still control where to apply forces. One misuse to watch for is applying physics directly inside the callback; prefer storing the intent and applying it in FixedUpdate so physics timing remains deterministic. After wiring these callbacks through PlayerInput → Invoke Unity Events, test with both keyboard and a connected gamepad to ensure composite bindings like WASD and left stick both produce the same Vector2 values.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › New Input Callbacks
Example callbacks
public void OnMove(InputAction.CallbackContext context)
{
    currentMovementInput = context.ReadValue();
}

public void OnJump(InputAction.CallbackContext context)
{
    if (context.performed && isGrounded)
    {
        rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
        isGrounded = false;
    }
}
Read the Vector2 in the callback and apply it during physics updates for consistent movement. Use context.performed when reacting to button presses.
Patterns
Store input values in fields inside callbacks, then in FixedUpdate compute a movement vector and call rb.MovePosition with Time.fixedDeltaTime to move the player reliably.
Misconception
Callbacks do not imply instantaneous physics application. Applying forces in callbacks can cause non-deterministic behavior; centralize physics in FixedUpdate.

screens.title: When to use Legacy vs New Input System
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between the legacy Input Manager and the new Input System depends on needs and scale. Use the legacy Input Manager for quick prototypes or simple single-player projects because it has a small A P I surface and immediate familiarity. The new Input System is preferable when you require remappable controls, multiple devices, or multi-player local device routing. It also offers cleaner separation of bindings from logic via Input Actions. A concrete use case: a four-player couch game with four gamepads is much easier to set up with the new Input System because each PlayerInput instance can be paired to a specific device. Conversely, if you're adding a simple jump and movement to a prototype, the legacy approach is faster. Migration considerations: avoid mixing both systems for the same actions, as that causes input conflicts. When installing the new package, accept the backend change; otherwise you may run both systems unintentionally. Performance is rarely a decisive factor; the new Input System provides better device handling and scales well for complex projects. Key takeaway: prefer the new Input System for projects that will need remapping, many devices, or robust action maps; keep the legacy A P I for one-off prototypes or when reading older codebases.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Hands-on Activity
Lab steps
  1. Create a Cube named Player and a Ground Plane. Add Rigidbody to Player and tag Ground as Ground.
  2. Create PlayerControls Input Actions asset. Add Gameplay map and Actions: Move (Vector2), Jump (Button).
  3. Add WASD composite and gamepad left stick to Move. Add Space and gamepad A to Jump.
  4. Attach PlayerInput to Player, assign asset, set Behavior to Invoke Unity Events.
  5. Create NewPlayerMovement script with OnMove and OnJump callbacks. Link events in PlayerInput inspector.
  6. Apply stored movement in FixedUpdate via rb.MovePosition and test the scene with keyboard and gamepad.
Starter code template
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

public class NewPlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5f;
    public float jumpForce = 10f;

    private Rigidbody rb;
    private Vector2 currentMovementInput;
    private bool isGrounded;

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent();
        if (rb == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("Rigidbody missing!");
            enabled = false;
        }
    }

    void FixedUpdate()
    {
        Vector3 moveDirection = new Vector3(currentMovementInput.x, 0, currentMovementInput.y);
        if (moveDirection.magnitude > 0)
        {
            rb.MovePosition(rb.position + moveDirection * moveSpeed * Time.fixedDeltaTime);
        }
    }

    public void OnMove(InputAction.CallbackContext context)
    {
        currentMovementInput = context.ReadValue();
        Debug.Log("Move input: " + currentMovementInput);
    }

    public void OnJump(InputAction.CallbackContext context)
    {
        if (context.performed && isGrounded)
        {
            rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
            isGrounded = false;
        }
    }

    void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
    {
        if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground")) isGrounded = true;
    }
}

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you will learn how Unity receives input from keyboards, mice, and gamepads, why input design matters for responsive gameplay, and when to choose the legacy Input Manager or the newer Input System package. We'll start from simple polling calls that are easy to add to small prototypes, and then transition to the Input Actions workflow that decouples bindings from game logic and scales to multiple devices. You will see concrete examples for movement and jumping, understand action maps and bindings, and complete a hands-on setup that uses the PlayerInput component to wire events to C# methods. By the end you will be able to implement basic player movement using either system, recognize common pitfalls like mixing systems or reading input in the wrong update loop, and choose an approach when you need remapping or multi-player device routing. Think about a simple cube that moves with WASD and jumps on space. That demo highlights practical trade-offs: the legacy A P I is quick to add, while the new system makes the project easier to expand and test across controllers. Keep that comparison in mind as we proceed.

These objectives frame the hands-on skills you will build. First, you will learn to use Unity's legacy Input Manager to capture basic keyboard, mouse, and gamepad input. That means recognizing polling methods, configuring axes, and wiring simple movement and button actions. Second, you will install and configure the new Input System package, create an Input Actions asset, and enable the runtime backend so your project can use action maps. Third, you will design Input Actions and Action Maps to separate bindings from game logic. That separation helps your code remain device-agnostic and makes remapping and multi-player routing easier. Fourth, you will handle the common input types — button presses, axes, and vector inputs — using both polling and event-driven approaches and then implement movement and jump actions driven by the systems we cover. Each objective includes a small rationale and a short mnemonic to help you recall the competency. Work toward the verified competency milestone by following the lab steps and implementing the provided code example.

This second objectives page expands each goal into a practical skill you will apply in the lab. First, capturing basic input via the legacy A P I means you can quickly poll keys and axes to drive movement. The skill here is to correctly use GetKeyDown for single-frame presses and GetAxis for continuous movement. A common mistake is reading GetKeyDown inside FixedUpdate; avoid that. Second, installing and configuring the Input System teaches you to create an Input Actions asset and accept the backend switch. This matters because it changes how Unity routes devices. Third, designing Action Maps and Actions is an organizational practice that keeps bindings separate from behavior; you will implement a Player action map for gameplay and a UI map for menus. Finally, handling inputs across polling and event-driven approaches will help you choose the right method for your gameplay and physics needs. Practice: wire Move as a Vector2 action, Jump as a Button action, and test them with both keyboard and gamepad. Each micro-mnemonic reinforces the competency so you can verify mastery in the hands-on steps.

The legacy Input Manager is Unity's built-in, polling-based input system. Polling means you ask the A P I each frame whether a key or button is down or whether an axis has a value. Common calls include GetKey, GetKeyDown, GetKeyUp, GetMouseButton variants, and GetAxis for named axes like Horizontal and Vertical. This system is fast to start with and good for small projects or prototypes where remapping and multi-device routing are not critical. A concrete example: you can poll Input. GetKeyDown for the space key to detect a jump press in the same frame it occurred. One important detail is that GetKeyDown and GetButtonDown are frame-based and should be read in Update so you don't miss presses. Areas where the legacy manager can cause friction include remapping, supporting many controllers, or splitting controls across many players; these require custom glue and can become error-prone. A common misconception is that GetAxis always returns immediate raw input; by default it smooths values, so GetAxisRaw exists when you need unsmoothed results. Key takeaway: use the legacy A P I for fast prototypes and simple single-player controls, but plan to move to the Input System if you need device-agnostic maps, remapping, or robust multi-player support.

A common source of bugs is mixing input polling timing with physics updates. Unity provides Update for per-frame logic and FixedUpdate for physics steps. For the legacy Input Manager, methods like GetKeyDown and GetButtonDown should be read in Update because they are frame-accurate. If you read them in FixedUpdate you risk missing presses because FixedUpdate may run fewer times per frame or at different intervals. For movement, a typical pattern is to read axis values in Update and store them, then apply movement in FixedUpdate where physics calculations happen. In the new Input System, event-driven callbacks deliver input events reliably and decouple when you read them from when you apply them. Still, apply physics changes like adding force or MovePosition in FixedUpdate, using the last known input state captured in a callback or stored in a field. A concrete pattern: capture the Vector2 movement from the Move action into a field, then in FixedUpdate construct a world movement and call rb. MovePosition with Time. fixedDeltaTime. A misconception to avoid is assuming callbacks automatically occur on the physics thread; they are still delivered on the main thread, so you must control where you apply forces. Key takeaway: read input at the right time, store intent, and apply physics in FixedUpdate to ensure deterministic simulation.

Axes are logical, named controls you configure in Project Settings under the Input Manager. A common axis is Horizontal which can aggregate multiple physical inputs: arrow keys, A/D, or a joystick X-axis. When you use Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") Unity returns a float between minus one and one. By default Unity applies smoothing to axis values, which helps make character movement feel less abrupt. If you need immediate, unsmoothed input for twitchy or pixel-precise controls, use Input. GetAxisRaw("Horizontal") which returns the raw device value. Another useful legacy pattern is to map a button to an axis name and use Input. GetButton or GetButtonDown with that name for actions. An important practical example: combining a keyboard composite and joystick axis under the same axis name lets you write movement code that is device-agnostic at runtime. The key misconception is assuming axis values are identical across devices; sensitivity and dead zone settings differ and must be tuned in the Input Manager. Key takeaway: axes simplify access to multiple bindings under a single name, but be deliberate about smoothing and tuning for responsiveness. Axes, GetAxis, and GetAxisRaw means use named axes to unify device inputs; choose getaxisraw when you need unsmoothed, immediate values for tight control.. In practical terms, how named axes work and when to use raw values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the provided LegacyPlayerInput example and highlight the teaching points. The script acquires a Rigidbody in Start and disables itself if absent — a defensive pattern to avoid null references at runtime. Input polling happens in Update because GetButtonDown and GetMouseButtonDown are frame-based queries. The code reads horizontal and vertical axes using Input. GetAxis and composes a move vector before applying Translate. For jump, the script checks Input. GetButtonDown("Jump") which maps to the spacebar by default in the Input Manager; the example then applies an impulse using AddForce on the Rigidbody. Mouse left-button polling uses Input. GetMouseButtonDown(0) to trigger a fire action. Notice that using transform. Translate for desktop-style movement is quick for simple prototypes but bypasses physics-driven movement; mixing Translate with physics bodies can produce non-physical results. If you want to apply forces or move a Rigidbody, do so in FixedUpdate using rb. MovePosition or AddForce. A common misconception is to treat Update and FixedUpdate interchangeably; they are not. The concrete takeaway: use Update to poll input, prefer physics APIs in FixedUpdate, and use the Rigidbody safely to manage colliders and forces. Try modifying the demo to use rb. MovePosition in FixedUpdate and observe collision behavior changes.

Transitioning to the new Input System begins with the Package Manager. Install the Input System package from the Unity Registry, accept Unity's prompt to enable the new input backend, and restart the editor if requested. This switches how Unity routes device input. Next, create an Input Actions asset in the Project window. The asset is where Action Maps, Actions, and Bindings live. Create an action map named Gameplay or Player for in-game controls, and add Actions like Move, Jump, and Fire. For Move, choose Action Type Value and Control Type Vector2; add a WASD composite and a gamepad left stick binding. For Jump and Fire choose Button type and add keyboard and gamepad bindings. Save the asset. A common misconception is that installing the package is enough; you must also enable the new backend when prompted or project input may still run through the legacy pipeline. Key takeaway: the new Input System is data-driven — the asset drives the runtime behavior, so organizing your Actions and Action Maps clearly up front simplifies wiring controls later with PlayerInput or code. Installing and setting up the New Input System means install package, accept backend switch, create input actions asset, define action maps, actions and bindings.. In practical terms, package install, enable backend, and create an input actions asset. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Each Action Map groups actions relevant to a context — for example, Player gameplay actions versus UI navigation. An Action represents a discrete game behavior like Move, Jump, or Fire. Actions have types; common choices are Button, Value, and Pass-Through. Bindings connect an action to physical controls such as keys, mouse buttons, or joystick axes. A Move action of type Value with control type Vector2 typically has a WASD composite binding and a separate binding for the gamepad left stick. This design separates control configuration from code: scripts respond to Action events or read Action values, and the same action can be re-bound without changing code. A useful analogy is thinking of Actions as public methods and bindings as the remappable keys that call them. A common misuse is scattering bindings across multiple assets or failing to group related actions into coherent maps, which hampers enabling or disabling sets of controls by context. Key takeaway: design clear action maps aligned with game states and keep action names meaningful so designers and programmers can collaborate without editing code.

The PlayerInput component simplifies using the new Input System. Attach it to your player GameObject, drag the Input Actions asset into the Actions field, and choose a Behavior. Behavior options include Invoke Unity Events, Invoke C# Events, and Send Messages. For beginners, Invoke Unity Events is easiest because you can link actions to public methods in the Inspector without writing event subscription code. After selecting Invoke Unity Events, expand the action map and add listeners for Move, Jump, and Fire, mapping them to methods like OnMove, OnJump, and OnFire on your player script. The PlayerInput component also automatically enables and disables the action map as the component toggles, helping with context switching. If you have multiple players, PlayerInput can be configured to pair with a specific device, which helps route each controller to the correct player. A misconception is thinking PlayerInput writes your callback wiring for you; it merely provides convenient event dispatch — you still implement the methods that react to those events. Key takeaway: PlayerInput makes wiring actions quick and supports different invocation patterns; use it to reduce boilerplate while you prototype action handling.

This walkthrough explains how a player script handles Input System callbacks. The example script stores the last Vector2 movement received in OnMove by calling context. ReadValue (). That value represents the player's intended horizontal and vertical motion. In FixedUpdate the script converts this Vector2 into a world-space vector and calls rb. MovePosition or uses AddForce for physics-based movement. For button-style actions like Jump and Fire, use context. performed to ensure you react only when the action is fully invoked, avoiding responded-to started or canceled phases. For Jump, check if the player is grounded before applying an impulse to prevent mid-air multi-jumps. Use OnCollisionEnter and OnCollisionExit to maintain a simple grounded flag. A common contrast with polling is that callbacks provide the exact moment of input and reduce the need to query every frame, but you still control where to apply forces. One misuse to watch for is applying physics directly inside the callback; prefer storing the intent and applying it in FixedUpdate so physics timing remains deterministic. After wiring these callbacks through PlayerInput → Invoke Unity Events, test with both keyboard and a connected gamepad to ensure composite bindings like WASD and left stick both produce the same Vector2 values.

Choosing between the legacy Input Manager and the new Input System depends on needs and scale. Use the legacy Input Manager for quick prototypes or simple single-player projects because it has a small A P I surface and immediate familiarity. The new Input System is preferable when you require remappable controls, multiple devices, or multi-player local device routing. It also offers cleaner separation of bindings from logic via Input Actions. A concrete use case: a four-player couch game with four gamepads is much easier to set up with the new Input System because each PlayerInput instance can be paired to a specific device. Conversely, if you're adding a simple jump and movement to a prototype, the legacy approach is faster. Migration considerations: avoid mixing both systems for the same actions, as that causes input conflicts. When installing the new package, accept the backend change; otherwise you may run both systems unintentionally. Performance is rarely a decisive factor; the new Input System provides better device handling and scales well for complex projects. Key takeaway: prefer the new Input System for projects that will need remapping, many devices, or robust action maps; keep the legacy A P I for one-off prototypes or when reading older codebases.

Follow this guided activity to implement player movement and jumping using the new Input System. Start a new 3D project or reuse an existing scene. Create a 3D Cube named Player and a Plane named Ground. Add a Rigidbody to the Player and ensure the Ground is tagged as Ground. Create a new Input Actions asset called PlayerControls and add an Action Map named Gameplay. Add Move (Value, Vector2) and bind a WASD composite plus a left-stick binding. Add Jump (Button) and bind Space and gamepad A. Save the asset. Attach a PlayerInput component to the Player and assign PlayerControls to its Actions field. Set Behavior to Invoke Unity Events. Create a NewPlayerMovement script and attach it to the Player. Implement OnMove to set a Vector2 field and OnJump to check context. performed and isGrounded before adding force. In FixedUpdate convert the stored Vector2 into a Vector3 and call rb. MovePosition with Time. fixedDeltaTime for smooth physics movement. Finally, in the PlayerInput component link Move and Jump events to the corresponding methods. Run the scene and test using both keyboard and an attached gamepad. The concrete outcome: a cube that moves with WASD or a stick and jumps with Space or the controller A button. Reflect: does the movement feel responsive? If not, tweak moveSpeed or use GetAxisRaw-like immediacy by adjusting bindings.

Keep three core concepts in mind. First, the legacy Input Manager is polling-based and suitable for simple prototypes; use GetKey, GetButtonDown, and GetAxis, and read frame presses in Update. Second, the new Input System uses Input Action Assets, Action Maps, Actions, and Bindings to separate configuration from code and support remapping and multiple devices. Third, timing matters: read inputs in the frame or via callbacks, store intent, and apply physics changes in FixedUpdate. These ideas will guide how you structure controls as your project grows and when you decide to migrate. Reflect: which concept will change how you design input for your next prototype?
